extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners in science communication, press officers, and journalists interested in health-related press release quality and its influence on news
extracted.subtask_short: evaluating health press releases for exaggeration
extracted.subtask_description: Methods and coding rules for identifying and measuring exaggeration in health-related press releases and their associated news articles (three types of exaggeration: advice, causal claims, and human inference from non-human studies). Includes sampling, coding, reliability and statistical-analysis standards for observational replication studies of press releases and news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advice coding categories (3 levels)
rubrics_metrics.description: Advice was coded at three levels. Advice was coded if it appeared anywhere in the title, abstract, or main text of the journal article, and in the titles or main text of press releases and news articles. If multiple pieces of advice appeared in an article, the strongest piece of advice was recorded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Categories listed in descending order of strength (higher entries trump lower): 'Explicit advice to reader'; 'Explicit advice not to reader'; 'No advice'. The strongest piece of advice in an article set is used. A press release or news article is deemed to have exaggerated advice if it contains a higher code than the corresponding peer-reviewed journal article. Note: authors acknowledge the operationalization of 'exaggerated advice' is problematic in some scenarios (e.g., justified readership change) and recommend caution when interpreting results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causal/correlational claims coding (seven-point scale)
rubrics_metrics.description: The strongest statements relating two variables in the study (e.g. a food and a disease) were recorded and coded on a seven-point scale to capture strength of causal language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seven-level hierarchy (descending strength): 'Cause'; 'Can cause'; 'Conditional cause'; 'Ambiguous'; 'Associative'; 'Does not cause'; 'No cause mentioned'. For journal articles the strongest claim was taken from the abstracts and discussion sections. For press releases and news the strongest statement was coded from the first two sentences of main text (excluding generic context leads). Only article sets where claims were based on correlational/observational data were included for this analysis. A press release or news article is classed as exaggerated if it contains a stronger (higher) category than the linked journal article. The authors note readers may not reliably distinguish between some middle categories (e.g., conditional, ambiguous, associative), and alternative codings (reader-understanding) may alter absolute exaggeration rates without changing core findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample coding (three-point: human/non-human/implicit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements about the sample were rated on a three-point scale describing whether the study/sample was presented as human, implicitly human, or non-human.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Categories (descending strength): 'Human'; 'Implicitly human'; 'Non-human'. Coding applied to statements about participant/sample type in journal articles, press releases and news. For the analysis of human inference exaggeration only journal articles with non-human samples were used to assess whether press releases or news made implicit or explicit human claims. A press release/news is judged exaggerated on sample if it has a higher sample code than the journal article (e.g., moves from 'non-human' to 'implicit human' or 'human').

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational definition of 'exaggeration'
rubrics_metrics.description: Exaggeration is operationalised as the press release or news article containing a higher-strength code than the corresponding peer-reviewed journal article for the dimension in question (advice, causal claim, or sample inference).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For each article set the strongest instance in each document is recorded and compared; if the press release/news has a higher (stronger) code than the journal article, it is marked as an exaggeration. Example: 'explicit advice to the reader' in a press release is deemed stronger than 'explicit advice, not to the reader' in a journal article. The authors note caveats to this rule (especially for advice) where changes may be justified by target readership or benign editorial decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Location rules for coding advice and causal claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Where to extract the text to be coded differs by document type and dimension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice: code if present anywhere in title, abstract, or main text of journal article, and in titles or main text of press releases and news. If multiple advice items appear, record the strongest. Causal claims: for journal articles use the abstracts and discussion sections; for press releases and news use the first two sentences of main text that are directly relevant to the research (exclude general contextual leads). These location rules are intended to capture the most salient statements for comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article inclusion and press-release selection criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Which press releases were eligible for the sample and how the sample was constructed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Press releases were collected from online repositories (universities' websites and EurekAlert) for members of the Russell Group (specific institutions listed). The sample period was January–June 2014 and January–June 2015. Press releases were restricted to those relevant to human health (broadly defined: biomedical, lifestyle, public health, psychological topics) that reported on a single, published, peer-reviewed research article. To avoid institutional imbalance a cap of 10 press releases per time period per institution (up to 20 per institution) was applied; selection where required was randomized.

rubrics_metrics.name: News article selection criteria (news linkage and timeframe)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules for which news articles to associate with each press release and the time window for capture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For each press release, relevant English-language top-tier international and national news outlets were searched via Google and the Nexis database up to 28 days after publication of the press release, and up to one week before (to allow for possible embargo breaches). Only news that referred to the source research were included.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding reliability and adjudication procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedures to ensure coding accuracy and to resolve disagreements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two researchers independently coded every article set (100% double coding). Codes were then compared electronically; coders met to discuss disagreements and reach consensus. On rare occasions where consensus was not readily reached, a third researcher made the deciding call. The coding sheet (questions and categories) used is provided in the open data accompanying the study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion criteria for causal-claim analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Types of studies excluded from the causal/correlational claim analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only cases where the design of the study reported in the journal article was observational (correlational) were included. Excluded designs: interventions (experimental), computer models/simulations, qualitative designs, and meta-analyses. This ensures the analysis tests exaggeration of causal language specifically in correlational research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis endpoints (three analytic aims)
rubrics_metrics.description: The study's predefined analytic goals for measuring relationships between press releases and news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three analyses were carried out: (1) quantifying levels of press release exaggeration for advice, causal claims, and human inference; (2) testing association of news exaggeration with press release exaggeration (whether press-release exaggeration predicts news exaggeration); (3) measuring news uptake (whether exaggerated press releases get more news coverage). These endpoints define primary outcome metrics and comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical analysis standard: use of GEE for clustered binary data
rubrics_metrics.description: Method for estimating associations and confidence intervals while adjusting for clustering (multiple news articles per press release, multiple press releases per institution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Generalised Estimating Equations (GEE) with a logit linking function for binary outcomes, and an exchangeable working correlation structure to account for clustering. GEE provides estimates and confidence intervals adjusting for correlated data within clusters; the exchangeable correlation assumes similar correlations between all data within clusters. This approach was implemented in SPSS v24 in the study. Authors suggest providing sufficient detail on equations and assumptions when reporting.
